title: The Day the Breeze Visited
markdown:
The sun, a soft warm peach, was just beginning to peek over Willow Creek Meadow, painting the sleepy world in apricot and rose. Cleo the squirrel, bright eyes wide with quiet observation, was already nestled on her favourite branch of the Whispering Willow. She held a dewdropped clover leaf, not as a microphone, but as something lovely to look at.

“Hello, meadow,” she murmured, voice a gentle whisper. “Today feels like a day for noticing new things.”

Below her, amongst the sturdy roots of the grand old oak, Mr Reed’s leaves rustled in a soft amused sigh. His voice, deep as wind through ancient branches, murmured, “A new thing, Cleo? It’s simply Tuesday. A perfectly lovely quiet Tuesday for a little rest.” Mr Reed had felt countless breezes, some soft and shy, others whisper-like, and he always enjoyed Cleo’s gentle observations.

Marn the mole, velvety nose twitching, poked his head out from his earth-scented burrow. He blinked behind spectacles perched rather precariously. “A… a visitor?” he whispered. “Oh dear. Will it be loud? Will it shake my burrow?” Marn was a creature of quiet habits and deep underground naps. Things that moved with unseen force always made him feel a little wobbly.

But Cleo, with a gentle twitch of her tail, was already sharing her quiet wonder. “Not a loud visitor, dear Marn. It’s a breeze. A visiting breeze. It’s come from afar. From lands of gentle mist. Listen now. Can you feel it approaching?” She held her breath, bushy tail still for a rare thoughtful moment, watching the distant hazy trees. “Yes. It’s here. A gentle wafting arrival. A whisper of cool air, like a soft velvet glove brushing your whiskers.”

As Cleo’s soft report reached the little folk of Willow Creek Meadow, a wave of quiet curiosity spread. A robin with a warm red breast tilted its head. A family of field mice peeked from their moss-lined nest. Soon Mrs Higgins the hedgehog, always eager to make her home welcoming, was carefully arranging her prettiest wildflowers by her front door. “Just in case,” she murmured, “the breeze wanted to admire them.” Young Freddie Fox sat quietly by the stream, watching the water.

The next day dawned clear and bright. “The breeze,” Cleo whispered, “continues its quiet visit. Today it brought a most delightful scent of blooming clover, wafting through the meadow like a sweet lullaby. A truly lovely perfume, wouldn’t you agree, Mr Reed?”

Mr Reed’s leaves shimmered. “Indeed, Cleo. It reminds me of summer mornings, long ago, when the world was full of soft secrets.”

Marn, a little braver, ventured further from his burrow. The breeze tickled his nose, carrying clover, and he found he rather liked it. He even let out a small happy sigh that puffed his cheeks. “It does smell rather nice,” he admitted, a shy genuine smile. The other meadow creatures, catching Marn’s less-worried tone, began to smile too. They started to pretend they were waiting for a special unseen guest, waving little leaves like tiny silent flags and humming soft welcoming tunes.

Cleo, seeing their shared delight, whispered with even more wonder, “And now the breeze seems to be practising its greetings. It’s rustling the leaves with a playful little dance. Like a silent song.”

By Thursday the whole town of Willow Creek was swept up in the charming charade. Fluffy-tailed rabbits practised gentle bowing, ears flopping with each dip. Bees hummed a special welcome tune. Even Bartholomew, the grumpy old badger, who usually preferred his solitude, was seen with a surprisingly clean broom, sweeping his doorstep with a determined air. “It’s like a quiet celebration,” whispered one of the field mice to her sister.

Then, on Friday, Cleo reported with a gentle pause, “A more vigorous gust has been observed. A momentary bluster. Hold onto your hats, everyone. Brace yourselves for a little playful fun.”

Marn squeaked softly, spectacles nearly slipping, as a stronger gust swept through. But the gust didn’t feel scary at all. It felt like a playful nudge, a friendly push that made him stumble just a little, then giggle. He even did a little skip. The wind swirled his spectacles, and when it passed he felt a lightness he hadn’t felt before, a bubbly feeling in his chest.

As the sun began to set on Saturday, painting the sky lavender and gold, Cleo delivered her final report, voice a little softer now. “And so, friends, the visiting breeze has completed its tour of Willow Creek Meadow. It leaves behind a sense of calm, a lingering sweetness, and the memory of its gentle presence.”

Mr Reed’s leaves whispered in the fading light. “Until next time, gentle breezes.”

Marn, no longer timid, sat on a smooth warm stone that still held the sun. He looked up at the first stars, tiny soft lights in deepening blue. Cleo scampered down her branch, tail still, a contented sigh escaping her. The whole meadow seemed to settle, a gentle hush wrapping the land.

“Everything was just right,” Marn whispered, a warm sleepy yawn escaping him. He curled up in his burrow, the cool earth a cozy blanket. He dreamt of breezes that tickled his nose, of happy greetings, and of being safe and warm. And soon everyone, from the smallest mouse to the oldest oak, drifted off to a peaceful slumber, their dreams filled with the quiet joy of an ordinary week that had felt, for a little while, like a visit.
characters: Cleo (a noticing squirrel), Marn (a quiet spectacle-wearing mole), Mr. Reed (an ancient-oak voice)
